clue.text: Brilliant contribution from Graeme Garden

indicators.note: the answer is a small part given by the words that follow

explanation.surface: Praise for a comedian's contribution to a show.
explanation.walkthrough: Graeme Garden is one of The Goodies, the 1970s British comedy trio this puzzle celebrates; the name looks like a tribute and is only a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang intensifier from Greek for 'great', used alone as an exclamation of praise, so a fair synonym.

clue.text: If you're not sure, keep it!

definitions.meaning: reads as doubt about a purchase or a decision
'it' is not a receipt but a mental attitude of staying undecided

explanation.surface: Advice to keep something in reserve when in doubt, like a receipt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep it' sounds like advice about a purchase you might return; the phrase is 'keep an open mind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not yet sure of their view keeps an open mind.

clue.text: Twice turn round and, losing heart, deny being pious

indicators.note: DENY drops its middle letters, keeping only its ends

parts.note: a turn = a go, as in 'whose go is it?'

explanation.surface: Someone turning round twice and rejecting any claim to religious devotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn round' looks like one instruction to reverse something, but it is two separate pieces, GO and O. 'Twice' tells you to repeat the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Goody-goody describes someone smugly virtuous, pious in a showy way.

clue.text: One of Barry, Robin or Maurice performing — what an animal!

parts.words: One of Barry, Robin or Maurice
parts.note: Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb were the Bee Gees

explanation.surface: A Bee Gee putting on a wild show, hailed as a real animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The three first names are the Bee Gees brothers, so any one of them is a GIBB. 'What an animal!' reads as a cheer and holds the plain definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is by category: this ape is one kind of animal, and 'what an animal!' is how you would cheer a wild performer.

clue.text: When at first you are getting frisky, position doesn't matter

indicators.note: frisky letters jump about into a new order
take the first letter of 'you'

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark that, when you're feeling frisky, any position will do.
explanation.walkthrough: The saucy surface keeps the eye on the bedroom; 'position doesn't matter' is a fair gloss of 'anywhere'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anywhere means in any place, so the position doesn't matter.

clue.text: Pale, stop messing around

indicators.note: the letters of STOP are messed about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone turned pale telling another to quit fooling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pale' pretends to be an adjective for a white face; here it is the noun, a fence stake, as in 'beyond the pale'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale is a wooden stake in a fence, which is a post.

clue.text: Position away from the freezer?

parts.note: what the freezer makes and holds

explanation.surface: Asking where to put something so that it is away from the freezer.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the answer, read in two parts, says where something is kept; the whole word means a post held by an official.
explanation.definitionFit: An office is a position of authority, as in 'the office of mayor'.

clue.text: Tire jack

definitions.meaning: as a verb: to grow weary, droop
a jack is the small ensign on a ship's bow, as in the Union Jack

explanation.surface: An instruction about lifting a car to change a wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a car tyre jack (American 'tire'); both words shift meaning, 'tire' to a verb and 'jack' to a ship's flag.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain synonyms: a verb meaning to lose energy, and a noun for the small banner a ship flies at its bow.

clue.text: Big Bang Theory's third on — spoil end of Netflix broadcast

indicators.note: the third letter of the word Theory is taken, as the possessive says
broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order
end of means the final letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: A TV fan grumbles that the third series of The Big Bang Theory is on, spoiling the end of a Netflix show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Bang Theory is a sitcom, which hides that Big Bang alone is the definition. The 'third' letter of Theory is E; ON, SPOIL and X (the 'end of' Netflix) are 'broadcast' to give XPLOSION.
explanation.definitionFit: The Big Bang is the cosmic explosion that cosmologists say began the universe.

clue.text: Refuse very noisily, with a look back around

indicators.note: around means the reversed word sits on either side of the other letters
back means the word is read from right to left

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look!
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Someone loudly refuses something while glancing back over their shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: Refuse is a noun here (rubbish), not the verb the surface suggests. 'look back' gives OL, and 'around' puts it either side of FF with A.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the waste parts of a butchered carcass, so it can mean rubbish or scraps in general.

clue.text: Dance about, get spotted

indicators.note: the letters of DANCE are moved about

explanation.surface: Dancing around in the hope of being noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get spotted' reads as 'be noticed' on the dance floor; 'spotted' here means covered in spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Acned means marked with acne, that is spotty.

clue.text: Wrong bits used to make part of a weapon

indicators.note: the letters are used as raw material to make something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Faulty components have been used in assembling a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Wrong looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder: WRONG and BITS together are 'used to make' something new.
explanation.definitionFit: The string of a bow is the cord that propels the arrow, so it is one component of an archer's weapon.

clue.text: Induce drummer to entertain battalion? Quite the reverse!

indicators.note: to entertain is to hold, so one part holds the other
swap the roles: the battalion holds the drummer

parts.note: Bn = battalion, the military abbreviation; the outer piece
Ringo Starr, the Beatles' drummer; goes inside

explanation.surface: Getting a drummer to put on a show for the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the drummer would hold the battalion; 'Quite the reverse!' swaps which piece goes outside. Ringo Starr is the standard crossword drummer.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring on something is to induce or cause it, as in 'bring on a headache'.

clue.text: Floods burrows

definitions.meaning: a bore is a tidal surge up a river, as on the Severn
to bore = to drill or tunnel

explanation.surface: Flood water filling animal burrows.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns about wet tunnels; 'burrows' is the verb, 'bores' as in drills.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidal bores are waves that flood upriver; a thing that burrows bores.

clue.text: 29s from first principles, as on the 17

indicators.note: 17 is RADIO, so the piece is as heard on the radio, by sound

explanation.surface: Working something out from the basics, as a radio presenter might.
explanation.walkthrough: 29 across is TRANSCEND, so '29s' is TRANSCENDS. 'The 17' points at 17 across, RADIO, which turns SEEDS into a spoken sound spelt CEEDS.
explanation.definitionFit: To transcend is to go beyond, which is to exceed.

clue.text: Slippery customer felt up in quite sweet surroundings

indicators.note: in means the reversed word is put inside the other
surroundings names the word that wraps around the reversed one

parts.note: cutish means rather cute, and cute means sweet

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

explanation.surface: A seedy encounter: someone groped in a cosy, sugary setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'felt up' reverses felt to give TLEF, which goes 'in' CUTISH, its 'surroundings'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cuttlefish is a slimy sea creature, and slippery customer is a jokey idiom for anyone hard to pin down.

clue.text: Spray a bit of scent on 3

indicators.note: only a small part, the first letter, of 'scent'

explanation.surface: Spritzing a little perfume on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spray' suggests perfume, backed by 'scent'; here it is a small bunch of flowers or leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A spray is a small branch of flowers or leaves, a sprig.

clue.text: Every so often, try and win on entertainment programmes here

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every second one

explanation.surface: Encouragement to enter competitions on game shows.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a phone-in quiz, which is fitting, since those are what you hear on the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio is where such entertainment programmes are heard.

clue.text: Award given to Taco Bell

indicators.note: the answer is held within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A British honour handed to an American fast-food chain.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour; the absurd image of a taco chain receiving one hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: The OBE is an award in the British honours system.

clue.text: Those restoring sight with chicken's heart and rabbit's foot could be witches

indicators.note: with here means the answer plus those letters, which together could be witches, so the letters are taken away

parts.note: witches are practitioners of the occult, occultists

indicators.note: the heart of chicken is its central letter

parts.note: chicken, whose heart is its middle letter

indicators.note: the foot of rabbit is its last letter

parts.note: rabbit, whose foot is its last letter

explanation.surface: Charms like a chicken's heart and a rabbit's foot suggest these healers might be dabbling in witchcraft.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it the other way round: the answer 'with' C (the 'heart' of chicken) and T (the 'foot' of rabbit) could be OCCULTISTS, so the answer is OCCULTISTS without them.
explanation.definitionFit: Oculists are eye doctors, specialists who treat the eyes and so help restore failing vision.

clue.text: Big build-up to the pair of us beginning to reconcile

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'reconcile'

explanation.surface: A long lead-up before a couple finally makes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big build-up' sounds like mounting tension; read literally it is something built up high.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: a tall building is literally something built up in a big way, not a crescendo of tension.

clue.text: White offspring of stallions and donkeys sounds like a horse

parts.note: W = white, as in chess notation
a hinny is the offspring of a male horse and a female donkey

explanation.surface: A white foal of mixed breeding that makes a horse's noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' is not a homophone signal here; it is the definition, a verb meaning neighs.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a verb phrase: to whinny is to make the high neighing noise a horse makes.

clue.text: Delivers uniform? By one report, but not according to me!

indicators.note: a report is what is heard, so the letter U is taken by its sound

parts.note: Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone disputing a claim about who delivers the uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Says you!' is a retort meaning 'that's your view, not mine', which the definition spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'says you' disputes a claim: that may be so for you, but not according to me.

clue.text: Esteban's really, really upset Japanese schoolgirl

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, bottom to top

parts.note: muy = 'very, really' in Spanish, Esteban being a Spanish name

explanation.surface: A Spanish man is very upset about a Japanese schoolgirl.
explanation.walkthrough: Esteban signals Spanish, where 'really' is MUY. Yum-Yum is one of the three schoolgirls in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado, set in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by character: she is one of the 'three little maids from school' in The Mikado, which is set in Japan.

clue.text: Oddie in front of Goodies line-up of stars

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'Goodies'

explanation.surface: Bill Oddie heading the cast list of The Goodies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goodies were Bill Oddie, Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor, a 1970s BBC comedy trio. 'In front of' looks like a position word but splits into IN and a first-letter signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Billing is the order in which performers are listed, a line-up of stars.

clue.text: One that writes about grams, a tonne, or an ounce?

parts.note: a Bic is a ballpoint pen

explanation.surface: A question about a writer covering units of weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Grams, tonne and ounce all look like weights; 'ounce' is also the snow leopard, which is why the question mark is there.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a big cat.

clue.text: Deploring mis-alignment?

indicators.note: mis-alignment tells you ALIGNMENT is mis-arranged

explanation.surface: Complaining about something being out of line.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits off 'mis', which acts as the signal and leaves the fodder whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamenting means expressing sorrow or regret, deploring.

clue.text: Spooner's to drop some pounds somewhere in Scotland

indicators.note: Spooner's version swaps the opening sounds of the two words, as the Reverend Spooner was said to do

parts.note: to drop weight you nosh (slang for eat) less: this part of the phrase gives nosh
the pounds you shed come from eating less: this part of the phrase gives less

explanation.surface: Someone talks of slimming in a Scottish location.
explanation.walkthrough: To drop some pounds you nosh less (nosh is slang for eat); say nosh as NOCH. 'Spooner's' treatment swaps the N and L sounds, giving the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous loch near Inverness, home of the legendary monster, is a place in the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: See 24 Down
Strong-smelling lubricant behind pleasurable activity

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the lubricant follows the activity

parts.note: KY Jelly, a brand of lubricant; placed behind FUN

explanation.surface: A smelly lubricant used during a bit of fun in the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: KY Jelly is a well-known brand of personal lubricant; the cheeky bedroom surface is deliberate, and the definition is the smell sense, not the music one.
explanation.definitionFit: Funky can mean having a strong, musty smell.

clue.text: 'Green sage stems in yogurt' and other delicious appetisers

parts.note: the stem, or first letter, of yogurt

indicators.note: the stems of these words are their starting letters, as the stem is where a plant begins

parts.note: first letters of other, delicious and appetisers

explanation.surface: A menu lists a green sage dish with yogurt among its tasty starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Green sage sounds like a herb on a menu, but it is the definition. The 'stems in' yogurt and the other three words (and is skipped) are their first letters, Y then ODA.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoda is the wise green Jedi master of the Star Wars films, small and famously sagacious.

clue.text: Hints and tips for Colin 'let's upset everybody' Sell

indicators.note: tips are the ends, here the first letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A mock nickname for Colin Sell, the pianist mocked on radio's I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Sell is the pianist on the BBC radio panel show I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue, where Goodies Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor starred; insulting him is a running gag.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with a nod to the theme: the radio show Colin Sell plays on is I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue.

clue.text: Go over Tim's head and screen performance lacking energy

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
a performance of these words puts their letters through a new routine, rearranging them
lacking means the letter for energy is missing from the rearranged letters

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone escalates a complaint above Tim, and also about a film performance short on energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim is Tim Brooke-Taylor, one of the Goodies, the theme; his 'head' is T. AND and SCREEN, 'lacking' one E, are given a 'performance' (rearranged) to make RANSCEND.
explanation.definitionFit: To transcend is to rise above or go beyond a limit, so it means to go over.
